text: Policy ID: POL-INV · Owner: Inventory & Supply Chain · Applies to: all dark stores · Version 1.0 (Apr 2025) This policy governs stock of focus SKUs in the Quick-Commerce Intelligence demo network (synthetic data).

The policy covers the 25 focus SKUs of each dark store: the store's most popular products, which drive most orders and availability complaints. 12 stores × 25 focus SKUs = 300 store × SKU pairs. Other products are replenished centrally and are outside this policy. The goal is simple: keep focus SKUs on the shelf without over-stocking. A stockout on a focus SKU is treated as a service failure, because the shopper may cancel the order or buy elsewhere.

Every focus SKU gets a risk tier each night, from closing stock, the reorder level and the demand forecast. High risk: stock is zero, or forecast demand over the next 3 days (supplier lead time of 2 days plus 1 day) is greater than or equal to the stock on hand. The SKU will very likely run out before a delivery can arrive. Medium risk: stock is at or below the reorder level, or less than 3 days of inventory remain. Low risk: none of the above. High-risk SKUs must be reviewed the same day. Medium-risk SKUs must be reordered in the next nightly cycle.

The reorder level of a SKU is set from its average daily demand: reorder level = 3 × average daily demand, rounded up, plus 1 unit. Stock is checked every night at 22:00 IST. When stock is at or below the reorder level and no delivery is already pending, a replenishment order is placed. Only one replenishment order may be open per store × SKU at a time. A SKU with fewer than 3 days of inventory (closing stock ÷ average daily units over the last 14 days) is reordered even if it is above its reorder level.

Stores replenish up to an order-up-to level: reorder level + 7 days of average demand + 2 units. When the forecast is available, the suggested order quantity is: forecast demand over the lead time and review period (2 + 1 days) + safety stock − current stock, rounded up and never negative. Safety stock = 1.65 × standard deviation of daily units over the last 28 days × √2, which targets a 95% service level. Suggested quantities are advisory: the store manager approves every order.

Suppliers deliver 1–2 days after an order is placed. Planning uses a 2-day lead time (the worst normal case). A delivery that has not arrived within 3 days is escalated to the supplier manager. During a known supplier outage, affected SKUs are marked High risk and substitutes are promoted in the app.

Each store counts every focus SKU once a week, on Monday at 06:00 IST. The count is the source of truth: calculated stock is reset to the counted figure. A gap between counted and calculated stock above 2 units for the same SKU in two consecutive weeks must be investigated. Damaged or expired units are written off on the day they are found and recorded as damage events; adjustments after a count are recorded as adjustment events.

A stockout day is any day on which a focus SKU's stock reached zero. Lost sales are estimated as the units the SKU normally sells on in-stock days (average of the previous 28 days) minus the units it actually sold, multiplied by the price. The estimate is reported before substitutes, so the store as a whole loses less. Stores with the highest lost sales are reviewed monthly.

More than 2 High-risk SKUs at one store at the end of a day: the store manager is notified. The same SKU out of stock on more than 3 days in a month: the reorder level is reviewed. A planned supplier outage: affected stores are told in advance and buffer stock is raised.

Policy ID: POL-DEL · Owner: Operations · Applies to: all dark stores and delivery partners · Version 1.0 (Apr 2025) This policy governs last-mile delivery in the Quick-Commerce Intelligence demo network (synthetic data).

Every order is promised within 15 minutes of pickup by the delivery partner. This is the delivery SLA (service level agreement). Typical delivery takes about 14 minutes, so the promise leaves little room: rain, traffic and peak hours push many deliveries past 15 minutes. The promise applies to every store and every order size.

On-time delivery rate = orders delivered within 15 minutes of pickup ÷ orders delivered. It is measured per store and per day. The 90th-percentile delivery time is also tracked, because the average hides the slowest deliveries. Failed deliveries and orders cancelled in transit are reported separately and are not counted as delivered.

A delivery is late when it takes more than 15 minutes from pickup. A delivery fails when the partner cannot hand over the order (customer unreachable, address issue). Customers with a late delivery are informed in the app; repeated lateness at a store is reviewed by operations. A failed delivery is returned to the store; prepaid orders are refunded under the Refund Policy.

Each store works with about 10 delivery partners. Only partners with an active status can be assigned orders. Partners are assigned in order of availability. A partner whose deliveries are repeatedly late is reviewed with the store manager.

Stores are reviewed weekly on: on-time rate, average delivery minutes, 90th-percentile delivery minutes, failed deliveries and in-transit cancellations. A store in the bottom three on on-time rate for two consecutive weeks must present an improvement plan, for example more partners at peak hours or a smaller delivery radius.

Policy ID: POL-CAN · Owner: Operations and Customer Service · Applies to: all orders · Version 1.0 (Apr 2025) This policy governs order cancellations in the Quick-Commerce Intelligence demo network (synthetic data).

A cancellation is classified by when it happens: Before dispatch (about 79% of cancellations): the order has not left the store. Stock is not consumed and no delivery is attempted. After dispatch (about 21%): the order is already with a delivery partner. The delivery is stopped and the goods return to the store. A normal cancellation rate is about 7% of orders placed. A store or day above 10% is investigated.

Every cancellation must record one reason. Before dispatch: customer changed mind, item unavailable, payment issue, duplicate order. After dispatch: delivery delayed, customer unreachable, address issue. Before-dispatch reasons are mostly customer-side; after-dispatch reasons are delivery-side and count against the store's delivery performance.

The customer is told about the cancellation in the app immediately, with the reason. When the store cancels because an item is unavailable, the app offers a substitute or a refund of that item. Prepaid orders cancelled after dispatch are refunded in full under the Refund Policy; cash-on-delivery orders are not charged.

Cancellations are reported weekly per store and reason, together with the share of orders placed. Item-unavailable cancellations are shared with the inventory team, because they usually point to a stockout. Delivery-side cancellations are reviewed with the delivery performance of the store.

Policy ID: POL-REF · Owner: Finance and Customer Service · Applies to: all prepaid orders · Version 1.0 (Apr 2025) This policy governs refunds in the Quick-Commerce Intelligence demo network (synthetic data).

A refund is issued when: a prepaid order is cancelled after dispatch: the full order amount is refunded; a delivered item is damaged, missing, of poor quality or expired: the amount of that item's line is refunded. Cash-on-delivery orders that were not delivered are not charged, so they need no refund. About 5% of orders lead to a refund.

Full refunds for orders cancelled after dispatch are issued within 48 hours of the cancellation. Item refunds must be requested within 72 hours of delivery and are issued once approved. A refund is recorded with a status (pending, completed or rejected); only completed refunds reduce revenue.

A refund can never exceed the payment it refunds. A refund record with an amount above the successful payment of its order is financially impossible: it is rejected by data quality checks and sent to quarantine, not counted. One order can have at most the payment amount refunded in total.

Net revenue = gross merchandise value − promotion discounts − completed refunds. Refunds are counted on the date the refund was made, not the date of the original order. For that reason, refunds are not included in average order value.
Policy ID: POL-PRO · Owner: Growth & Marketing · Applies to: all promotions · Version 1.0 (Apr 2025) This policy governs promotions in the Quick-Commerce Intelligence demo network (synthetic data).

Promotions are category-wide percentage discounts (for example "Dairy 15% off") that run in all stores for a fixed window. Every promotion needs approval from the marketing manager before it starts, with its category, discount, start date and end date. About 20% of orders use a promotion.

Discounts are set in steps of 5%, from 5% to 30%. A discount above 30% is not allowed; a promotion record outside 0–100% is invalid and rejected by data quality checks. A promotion runs for 3 to 14 days. Only one promotion per category may run at a time.

Uplift compares the promoted category's average daily units (all stores) during the promotion with its average on days without any promotion: uplift % = (promotion daily units − baseline daily units) ÷ baseline × 100. Discount cost is the total discount given on completed orders that used the promotion. This is a before / after comparison, not a controlled experiment: seasonality, weather and other events also move sales.

Every promotion is reviewed after it ends, on uplift, discount cost and orders that used it. A promotion with negative uplift, or uplift too small to cover its discount cost, should not be repeated in the same form. Deal-seeking customers respond most to promotions; premium customers respond least, so promotions are better targeted at deal-seeking segments.
Metric: Completed order; Definition: An order that was delivered, has a successful payment and was not cancelled.; Formula: slvorders.iscompleted.

Metric: Line revenue; Definition: Revenue of one order line. Uses the catalog price when the line's unit price was flagged (dqunitpricemismatch), otherwise the recorded line amount.; Formula: quantity × (catalog price if flagged else unitprice).
Metric: GMV; Definition: Gross merchandise value of completed orders, before discounts.; Formula: Σ line revenue (completed orders).
Metric: Discount; Definition: Promotion discounts on completed orders.; Formula: Σ orderpromotions.discountamount (completed orders).
Metric: Refunds; Definition: Refunds with status completed, counted on the refund's business date.; Formula: Σ returnsrefunds.amount where status = completed.
Metric: Net revenue; Definition: What the business keeps.; Formula: GMV − Discount − Refunds.
Metric: Order value; Definition: Value of a completed order at checkout.; Formula: order GMV − order discount.

Metric: Average order value (AOV); Definition: Average checkout value of completed orders. Refunds are not included because they are dated by refund date, not order date.; Formula: (GMV − Discount) ÷ completed orders.
Metric: Units; Definition: Items sold in completed orders.; Formula: Σ quantity (completed orders).
Metric: Orders placed; Definition: Every order in Silver, whatever its outcome.; Formula: count(orders).
Metric: Cancellation rate; Definition: Share of placed orders that were cancelled.; Formula: cancelled orders ÷ orders placed.
Metric: On-time delivery rate; Definition: Share of delivered orders delivered within the SLA (15 minutes from pickup).; Formula: delivered with deliveryminutes ≤ 15 ÷ delivered.
Metric: Units sold (inventory); Definition: Units leaving stock: every order line of a focus SKU except orders cancelled before dispatch.; Formula: Σ quantity (orders not pre-dispatch cancelled).

Metric: Days of inventory; Definition: How many days the closing stock lasts at the recent sales rate. Empty when there were no sales in the last 14 days (never infinite).; Formula: closing stock ÷ average daily units sold (last 14 days).
Metric: Stockout day; Definition: A day on which a focus SKU's stock reached zero at any point.; Formula: min stock during the day ≤ 0.

Metric: Lost sales (estimate); Definition: Units and revenue a focus SKU would have sold on its stockout days. Revenue lost for that SKU, before any substitute the shopper bought instead.; Formula: max(0, avg daily units on in-stock days of the previous 28 days − units sold) × catalog price.
Metric: Bulk order; Definition: An order with any line of 8 or more units (normal lines are 1–5).; Formula: max(quantity) ≥ 8.

Metric: Support / confidence / lift; Definition: Basket association between products A and B over completed orders.; Formula: support = baskets(A∧B) ÷ baskets; confidence(A→B) = baskets(A∧B) ÷ baskets(A); lift = confidence(A→B) ÷ (baskets(B) ÷ baskets).

Model: Baseline: seasonal naive; How it forecasts: same weekday one week earlier. Model: Baseline: moving average; How it forecasts: mean of the last 7 days (flat for all 7 days ahead). Model: Main model; How it forecasts: one HistGradientBoostingRegressor across all 240 series, Poisson loss (daily unit counts). Model: Uncertainty band; How it forecasts: two more gradient-boosting models with quantile loss (10th and 90th percentile). Features (17): lag 1/7/14, rolling mean 7/14, rolling std 7, day of week, weekend, holiday, month, day of month, promotion active, rainfall, temperature, yesterday's stockout share, store, category. Stockout days are down-weighted in training (weight = 1 − 0.5 × stockout share), because sales on those days understate real demand. Recursive multi-day forecasting: for day 2–7 the model's own forecasts fill the lag / rolling features, which is exactly how the forecast is used live.

The backtest model (trained on Apr–Aug) forecasts 1–7 days ahead from every day of September: 45,360 forecasts next to the actuals and both baselines. Metrics: MAE, RMSE, WAPE (Σ|error| ÷ Σ actual, the headline), bias, and band coverage. Rule from the plan: the model counts as useful only if it beats both baselines on WAPE.

What did empty shelves cost us, and which SKUs did it hit hardest? An inventory manager is judged on availability. The lost-sales figure turns stockouts into money and tells the manager where better replenishment would pay off. The explorer lets them drill into one store × SKU to see why it ran out.

For every stockout day (stock reached 0 at some point, from gldinventorydaily): expectedunits = average daily units sold on the SKU's IN-STOCK days in the previous 28 days lostunits = max(0, expectedunits − units actually sold) lostrevenue = lostunits × catalog price Stockout days are excluded from the expectation, because their sales were cut short by empty shelves and would drag the expectation down. At least 7 in-stock days of history are required; otherwise no estimate is made. Business caveat: in the simulation a shopper facing an empty shelf often bought a substitute, so this is revenue lost for that SKU. The store as a whole lost less.

Each detector compares an observed count with what is normal over the previous 28 days and scores how unlikely the count is (p-value, shown as score = −log10 p). An anomaly is a signal to investigate, not proof of a problem. Detector: Demand spike; Observed: orders containing a product at a store on a day; Expected: product's share of the store's orders over the last 28 days × that day's store orders; Flag when: p < 0.0001 and ≥ 4 orders; consecutive days merged. Detector: Payment failure; Observed: network-wide failed payments and payment-service ERROR logs per hour; Expected: same hour, previous 28 days; Flag when: p < 0.000001 and ≥ 4 events; consecutive hours merged. Detector: Store outage (experimental); Observed: orders in a 2–8 hour window (06:00–23:59 IST); Expected: same store, hours and day type (weekday/weekend), previous 28 days; Flag when: p < 0.001 and ≥ 6 orders expected.

section: Anomaly detection (5C) › Method revision (approved 2026-10-05, after the first measurement)
text: The first version used Poisson p-values, which assume the variance equals the mean. The data varies much more than that: store-day orders have a mean of 15.6 and a variance of 27.7, driven by weekdays, rain and promotions. Ordinary quiet or busy spells therefore looked "impossible", and the first measurement failed precision (7 of 30, 23%). Changes, all decided before re-measuring once: 1. Spikes and outages use a negative binomial model (var = μ + α·μ²), with α estimated from the data by method of moments. 2. The spike baseline scales with that day's store orders, so a busy day is not a spike. 3. Store outages are labelled experimental and left out of the precision figure. A store gets less than 1 order an hour, so a 3–6 hour outage cannot be told apart from chance using orders alone. Real systems use store heartbeats, which this data does not have. 4. Thresholds, minimum counts and the pass bars were not changed. Payment detection was unchanged (it had passed).

section: Anomaly detection (5C) › Verification against the planted anomalies
text: Pass bars were fixed before measuring. A detection matches a planted anomaly with the same type, store and product within 1 hour (1 day for spikes). Check: 5C.2 Demand spikes found (≥ 80%); First run: 4 of 6; After revision: ⚠️ LIMIT: 4 of 6, known limitation. Check: 5C.3 Payment failures found (≥ 2/3); First run: 3 of 3; After revision: ✅ PASS: 3 of 3. Check: 5C.4 Store outages (no bar, reported); First run: 0 of 6; 11 false alarms; After revision: 0 of 6; 5 false alarms. Check: 5C.5 Precision of spike + payment detections (≥ 50%); First run: 23% (all detectors); After revision: ✅ PASS: 7 of 11 (64%). Why 5C.2 is not met. Both missed spikes are undetectable from this data: S02 / P0062 on 4 April is day 4 of the data, so there is no 28-day history to compare with. S11 / P0282 on 23 July was planted as "~25% of orders" but produced only 3 orders at that store, below the 4-order minimum. Lowering the minimum would flood the list with 3-order false alarms. The bar stays and the result is reported as LIMIT.

Anomaly p-values are per-test; with thousands of store × product × day tests a few false alarms are expected (4 of 11 here). Store outages from order volume alone are not reliable at ~1 order per store-hour. Weekly delivery and cancellation tables are matched to the filter by week, not exact days.
